utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Starting, as I say, with the most important person, our Case Manager, Sebastiaan van Hooydonk; Joanna Korner and Matthew Olmsted for this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic, and Andreja Zecevic, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, Michelle Butler, Lennart Poulsen, David Martini, and Miroslav Cuskic with Joyce Boekestijn, appearing for Zupljanin Defence today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm so sorry, I forgot to mention that our intern, Lucy Eastwood, who is gripped by these proceedings, is back today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that when we took the adjournment yesterday, Mr. Krgovic was about to hand over to Mr. Aleksic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Thank you, Your Honours. In the first part of my presentation, I'm going to deal with the credibility of some of the Prosecution witnesses. And since a majority of them provided their in testimonies in closed sessions or private sessions or they had protective measures granted to them, I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to move into private session for a moment so that I can proceed talking about those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something about the testimony of Witness Jovicinac briefly. Witness Jovicinac was, as he himself put it, born in 1949. He graduated from textile industry high school and then military high school and he graduated from the Faculty of Law in 1986, which means when he was 37 years old. Prior to 1992, he did not discharge any duties within the ambit of the military judiciary, i.e., either military courts or military prosecutor's offices; in other words, he had no previous experience whatsoever. As for his testimony, the witness denied ever having seen document P1284.10, namely guide-lines for the work of military prosecutor's offices issued by the prosecutor's office attached to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. These guide-lines, at pages 15 of the Serbian version and 9 of the English read, and this is the chapter dealing with crimes against humanity and international law. And it reads: "In order for the command of the Main Staff to have full insight into the type and number of these crimes, all unit commands shall be duty-bound to work toward uncovering all cases of war crimes against humanity and international law in the areas of their responsibility." Furthermore, on two occasions the witness asked from the investigating judge to secure the release of suspects who were suspects of -- of suspect perpetrators of some of the most serious war crimes. One of them is P1284.38. This is the case of the killings in Velagici. So this witness agreed that they be released from mandatory detention and the crime -- the crime in Velagici is something that Mr. Zupljanin is charged with. And, finally, let me speak about the testimony of Mr. -- or Comrade Dragicevic, as he wanted to be addressed during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this, Mr. Aleksic. Before we proceed to the next witness, I'm not sure I fully understood the impact of -- of your presentation regarding this witness. You said that he had never seen the guide-lines for the work of military prosecutor's office and that he had then asked the investigating judge to secure the release of two suspects. What is the implication of that? Can you just clarify briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he performed the duty of the military prosecutor at the time. And in the context of him never having seen such a document, how was he able to perform the duty of a Military Prosecutor; this being one of the basic documents governing their work under those circumstances? That was the meaning of my submission. And as for ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So your point is that -- that this gentleman was incompetent as a Military Prosecutor; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As for this other case, he broke the Law on Criminal Procedure. He even asked that the criminal proceedings against these individuals be stayed or suspended. There was a term that, in the B/C/S, does not even exist in the legislation, and this is quite apart from the fact that he asked that these individuals be released. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As for Witness Radulovic, he testified extensively. I would ask Their Honours to carefully examine his testimonies, both his answers given on direct examination and cross-examination. In great many of these answers, he changed his position. I would also suggest that Their Honours analyse in parallel the testimony of Witness Sajinovic and Witness Radulovic. Witness Sajinovic on the issue of some of the very important issues, such as the establishment and the method of work of the Milos Working Group, who their sources of information were and when and how they forwarded information to Mr. Zupljanin, the answers differ from the answers provided by Witness Radulovic. I would now like to address the portion of the Prosecution final trial brief where it is stated that Mr. Zupljanin had effective control. Our learned friend Ms. Butler said something about it. Our position is quite the opposite for a number of reasons; Mr. Zupljanin did not have effective control. In paragraph 843 of the final trial brief of the Prosecution, it is stated that one of the ways in which Mr. Zupljanin exercised his control was by asking to be regularly informed by his subordinates, and reference is made to document P374. In our view, the document lends support to our case. The reason why the document was sent was due to the fact that there was no thorough or regular reporting, and that is why at one point Mr. Zupljanin said, Daily reporting by the SJB to the operations duty officers of the CSB BL on important events is riddled with shortcomings and faults, and they consist of the following, and there follows a list of these. In his testimony, Witness SZ-003 stated that standard practice and procedures governing reporting were not always adhered to in terms of the accuracy of information or timeliness, some of the dispatches were incomplete, some of the incidents were not reported on at all or were not reported on in time, and some people were not diligent enough in compiling these reports. And this can be found at transcript page 24399 to 24400. At paragraph 844, the Prosecution say that, in addition the written correspondence, Mr. Zupljanin attended meetings, and mention is made of the 11th of July meeting and his -- his words about the rounding up of the Muslims and their detention in -- in camps. Let's look at what it is exactly that Zupljanin said at this meeting. Namely, that the army and the Crisis Staffs, or, rather, the War Presidencies were asking that as many Muslims be gathered but they say that the conditions in these camps are poor, there is no food and some individuals do not respect international norms, et cetera. This will be discussed further later on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- also confirmed that. As for these --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt again. The witness just mentioned was protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I just said strike it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You did?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. As for the dispatch in document P535 which Zupljanin forwarded to the chiefs of the -- of the SJB in which it is noted that all the employees have to sign the solemn oath, it should be noted that it was forwarded on the basis of a dispatch written by Mr. Mandic, which is P535, which was not intended as a means of discrimination against non-Serbian population but, rather, the means of implementing the law of the new state, as the constitution had been declared and the Law on Internal Affairs had come into force at the time. The Prosecution witness Tutus confirmed this argument, saying that the new solemn oath was no different from the previous one which was in force during the SFRY and which all the police employees were also obliged to sign. What is important is that Mr. Zupljanin advocated multi-ethnicity which can be found in P5353 under item 2 which says: "It is in our interest to preserve the ethnic composition of employees in the SJB in accordance with the ethnic composition of the population in the municipality." Further, it is not correct that Mr. Zupljanin was aware of what was going on in Sanski Most as expressed in this paragraph. The Defence claims that it was only on the 9th of September, 1992, that in the dispatch which he -- Witness ST-161 sent, Zupljanin learned from this dispatch that the policemen from that SJB were resubordinated to the army in Manjaca. We will discuss this document later on in further detail. There is no evidence that the chief of the SJB from Kotor Varos, Savo Tepic, ever personally visited Mr. Zupljanin. ST-167, on the contrary, testified that for Tepic this was just an excuse to leave Kotor Varos for private reasons. That is T12417. In paragraph 848, it is claimed that Drljaca was a close associate of Mr. Zupljanin who carried out his orders and reported to Mr. Zupljanin. As for the situation in Prijedor and the role of the Crisis Staff, the local commanders of the VRS and their influence on the operation of the SJB, the SJB Prijedor - we will discuss that in more detail later on - but I may say that because of all this the Prijedor SJB was completely independent and was acting without any influence from the Banja Luka CSB. Prosecution witness Gajic confirmed that during the indictment period the SJB chiefs often acted beyond the framework of their duties, that they refused to obey Zupljanin's orders and instead acted in accordance with the orders of the local Crisis Staffs, or, rather, the army which can be found on page 12910. He especially emphasised that the SJB Prijedor disobeyed. It was evident that Simo Drljaca was not implementing the decisions of the Banja Luka CSB which is page 12910 and 14. Witness Macar, who was a high ranking employee of the Republican Ministry of the Interior at the time, also testified that on the occasion of his visit to Prijedor, Drljaca told him that neither the Banja Luka CSB nor the Ministry of the Interior was superior to him, i.e. to Drljaca, and that his real superiors were the municipal Crisis Staff and the municipal authorities, which can be found on pages 22972 through to 79 of the transcript. The fact that testifies to Zupljanin's lack of authority for relieving Drljaca of his post is that the local municipal assembly from Prijedor relieved Drljaca of his duty in 1993 only after Mr. Krajisnik, who was the parliament Speaker at the time, had visited Prijedor. And even though our colleagues said yesterday that there is no evidence of that in the case file, I would like to point out to the Trial Chamber that Prosecutor witness Miskovic talked about that at transcript page 15273. As for the problems relating to the conduct of Mr. Drljaca, Mr. Zupljanin discussed that with Prosecution witness Radulovic. He informed him that it was impossible to remove Drljaca, that there had been various attempts to do so by some armed groups but that they had all been unsuccessful because Drljaca was simply too powerful because of his close relations with the local Crisis Staff and the local commanders of the VRS. Radulovic further testified that the removal of Drljaca from his power base in Prijedor would be -- would have a very uncertain outcome and could cause even more problems, which can found on transcript page 11088. As for the situation in Prijedor we should take into account that 612 policemen from the SJB Prijedor were resubordinated to the army, the local brigades in combat operations, without any approval of the Banja Luka CSB. P689 is the reference. In paragraphs 856, 857 and 862, of its final brief, the Prosecution claims that Zupljanin did not take my measures to take disciplinary proceedings against policemen nor did he file criminal reports against them. The Defence refers to a section of its final brief where we deal with Count 12(g) of the indictment and where we clearly show that what the attitude of Mr. Zupljanin was. Further, the Prosecution claims that -- that can be found in paragraphs 864 through to 867, 869 and 870, they claim that Crisis Staff did not influence Mr. Zupljanin's effective control or reduce it. We invite the Trial Chamber to review section 12 B of our final brief, where we deal with this topic. Many Prosecution witnesses testified that the municipal Crisis Staffs frequently, together with the army, usurped Mr. Zupljanin's ability to issue orders that would be complied with. It is mentioned there that Mr. Zupljanin forwarded some decisions of the Crisis Staffs but we claim that in his dispatches, Mr. Zupljanin forwarded the decisions of government organs which were in accordance with the law, as, for example, P594 and P1883 show. In Exhibit P594, this is a decision that no one is allowed to leave the territory of Krajina carrying an amount more than 300 Deutschemarks without a certificate from a bank that the money was taken from the bank. We claim that such a law had already existed in the former Yugoslavia and that the objective was to prevent money being taken out from the country. Similarly, P1883 was an enactment whose purpose was that able-bodied men, regardless of their ethnicity, should not avoid their legal duty and that they should respond to mobilisation call-ups. Paragraphs 871 to 881 of the Prosecution trial brief once again contains the claim that the VRS did not reduce Mr. Zupljanin's effective control. We discuss that in detail in our final brief. And as for resubordination, the position of the Defence is completely clear. During the trial, the evidence showed without any doubt that resubordination was the factual situation which was caused by the principle of the singleness of command. We will discuss this further a bit later on. Let me just point out that Expert Kovacevic so discussed that, so did the Trial Chamber witness Lisica, and we should note that these positions of the Defence were confirmed by many Prosecution witnesses. We discuss that in detail in paragraphs 222 through to 228 of our final brief. Further on, in paragraph 875 of its final brief, the Prosecution claims that Mr. Zupljanin distinguished between policemen who were resubordinated to the army and were involved in combat activities and those who were not resubordinated. They give reference to Exhibit P624. Reading this document in detail and analysing it shows clearly that Mr. Zupljanin had in mind, on one hand, the policemen who had been resubordinated to the army in combat operations, and, on the other hand, members of the police who had been permanently assigned to the army; that is to say, they were not members of the police anymore but they had rather become members of the army and had different tasks. As for resubordination, my learned friends from the Prosecution changed their position over the last few days and said that even if this did happen, that is to say, even if police members had been resubordinated to the army, the resubordination only had to do with combat operations on the front line. Prosecution witness Krejic talked about this, and he was the SJB chief in Skender Vakuf. On pages T14042 and 043, he said that at the time in August 1992 one of his units was resubordinated to the local VRS brigade and that the only task of this unit was to secure a certain road. As for the tasks which the resubordinated policemen had to carry out, we should pay attention to Exhibit P5613 [as interpreted] dated the 18th of September, 1992, in which Mr. Zupljanin -- I apologise. We're talking about the 18th of September, 1992. And it is a document in which Mr. Zupljanin says that there are problems and that outside the knowledge of the chief of the SJB and CSB, policemen are engaged in combat operations. In accordance with the agreement with the highest ranking representatives of the army, it was necessary, as he says, and the situation is repeated even in September 1992. As for the communications system and how it operated, this is discussed in paragraphs 881 through to 886 of the Prosecution final brief. My learned friends touched upon that yesterday. Witness ST-167 who is an expert in this field, when presented with Exhibit P1468 which is one of the reports for the year 1992, the witness testified that the statistics show that there was a sharp drop in the number of sent and received dispatches in the period between the 11th of June and the end of 1992, and that that also refers to the exchange of dispatches between the Banja Luka CSB and the Kotor Varos SJB. Prosecution witness Kezunovic, confirmed that in Exhibits P595 and P621 contain precise statistics about the number of dispatches sent during the first six months of 1992 and also the period between the 1st of July and 30th of September, 1992. My learned friend Mr. Krgovic talked about that yesterday so let me not repeat that. But I will say that the significance of these numbers is emphasised in the report in the number of dispatches sent in the first nine months of 1991. That report contains the total number of more than 200.000 dispatches sent and received. Even though the Prosecution claims that there is no evidence for this position, except from the testimony of Witness Kezunovic, we point to Exhibit 2D52, which is a report on the work of the Banja Luka CSB for the first nine months of 1991, in which on page 12 - in English version it's page 11 - it says that the total number of the received dispatches is 188.168 and those that were sent were 39.858. It should be noted that this information covers 15 SJBs which belong to the CSB at the time, as opposed to the 26 SJBs which were part of the CSB in 1992. This was also discussed by the Prosecution witness Rakovic who explained the problems which existed in Banja Luka and the entire Krajina area. There were periods when the electricity was down for two months in Banja Luka and no fuel was available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic, I'm sorry to interrupt to you. Our legal officer just drew the Chamber's attention to something that you said in relation to -- to an exhibit. It's page 20, line 8, and the transcript records that you referred to an Exhibit P5613. I don't think we got that far. We got far enough, for sure. But we didn't raise it until -- to the 5.000s.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honours. It was a mistake. It is Exhibit P613.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And, again, please forgive me for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Due to the shortage of time I cannot go into great detail on the issue of communications, but I would like to say that Mr. Zupljanin at the collegium meeting which was held on the 11th of July, 1992, in Belgrade said that the main communications system had been destroyed. Furthermore, when it comes to reporting, the Prosecution says that the -- that Mr. Zupljanin received reports drafted by the Milos Group and this doesn't arise from either the testimony of Mr. Radulovic or the testimony of the Defence witness Sajinovic who said that the Milos Group reports were not sent to their superiors but, rather, they were sent to the CSB in Belgrade. This is on page 25120. To corroborate this part of Sajinovic's testimony, I would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to P1328.13. This is an Official Note which was drafted in 1993 at the state security CSB Banja Luka and in which it says something about the establishment of the Milos Group, and I quote: "Bearing in mind that over two years ago we were officially established as a group intended for co-operation with the MUP of Serbia, we had an occasion on several occasions to spend some time and get in touch with the colleagues in the MUP of Serbia. From the beginning, we agreed amongst ourselves that we will focus our interest on collecting intelligence about the enemy armed formations, the enemy intelligence services, associates, and other collaborators of the enemy," and so on and so forth. In paragraphs 891 to 909 of the Prosecutor's final brief, there is a reference to the information that Mr. Zupljanin had with regard to detention centres. In paragraph 891 there's a reference to a document which is P1560. We claim that the introduction into this document says -- or, it arises from that introduction that that decision was in keeping with the decision of the municipal Crisis Staff in Prijedor and that the purpose of that decision was to detain people who were captured in combat and who had to be interviewed. The Defence repeats and reiterates its position that the tone, the language, and the official nature of this order points to the fact that this was a military facility. Moreover, it arises from the testimony of Mr. Radulovic on page 11126 that Mr. Drljaca bypassed Mr. Zupljanin and he deprived him of any information. Furthermore in paragraph 891, the Prosecution claims that in May Radulovic twice reported on -- the problem of the mass arrests of the non-Serbian population and that the detainees were not provided with adequate food or accommodation. The Prosecution refers to two reports and by the Milos Group, and I already said that there is no single piece of evidence to the effect that those reports were ever sent and that Mr. Zupljanin received the Milos Group reports. As for the crimes committed in certain detention centres, and Mr. Zupljanin's knowledge about that, a lot was said about that in our final brief. I would like to add to what was already said, that Zupljanin did not know anything about those crimes. Our thesis was corroborated by the fact that the information that he received from Radulovic, and our learned colleagues said that that had happened several days before the collegium meeting on the 11th of July, and that he immediately reported that to the collegium, and he demanded that measures should be taken. In August, he set up a commission whose task was to examine the conditions and the treatment of the detainees in those facilities. This you will find in P601 on the revisited issue of that commission a bit later. Zupljanin's lack of knowledge about the events in Prijedor was testified about by Witness ST-241. He was one of the employees of the National Security Service and, as such, he was sent to Omarska. The witness testified that there were never any contacts between the operatives who participated in interviewing the suspects in Omarska and Mr. Zupljanin. You will find this on page 16745. Zupljanin's lack of knowledge about the conditions in Omarska is corroborated by document P1560. It is stated in this order: "I strictly forbid conveying information of any sort with regard to the functioning of this collection centre. All official documentation has to be kept at the centre and it cannot be -- it cannot be taken out of the centre or destroyed without the approval of the chief of the police station in Prijedor." Drljaca emphasised the weight of any breach of this order and he added that he demands all the personnel, and especially authorised officials, to strictly adhere to the instructions provided herein. When it comes to the allegations in paragraph 9002, according to which Mr. Zupljanin visited Omarska twice, save for the testimony of Witness ST-23 there is no other evidence. I have already addressed the credibility of this witness, so I wouldn't want to waste any more time on that. Witness Jankovic testified that before the arrival of the delegation to Omarska on the 14th of July, Drljaca had rearranged conditions in the prison. Because of that delegation, Miskovic admitted that the detainees had looked unkempt and that they had not been clean shaven, and Zupljanin drew everybody's attention to everybody at the meeting on the 11th of July. In any case, he did not mention any signs of physical maltreatment. Srdic, the president of the Red Cross in Prijedor, confirmed that the Red Cross had opportunities to visit the prisoners and bring them food and medicines. When it comes to paragraph 904, it is stated in that paragraph that General Talic stated that no single soldier was informed in the massacre at Keraterm on the 25th of July. The position of the Defence is that we do not challenge the fact that there was indeed crime committed against the prisoners in Keraterm, including also the murder in room 3. Prosecutor Witness ST-151, who was at Keraterm at that time, stated that people who stormed into the room 3 were not guards but soldiers who had arrived from outside, and those who controlled Keraterm and Trnopolje wore olive-drab and camouflage uniforms. This was subsequently confirmed by Prosecutor Witness ST-183. He stated that Colonel Arsic had taken over command in Prijedor and subordinated local police forces. When it comes to a paragraph 913, we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Paragraph 919.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We contest the allegations in this paragraph where it is stated that at the beginning of -- at the end of July or beginning of August Radulovic informed Zupljanin about a meeting in Teslic. Amongst others, Generals Mladic and Lisica were also there and the leadership of the army ordered the local police to expel the non-Serbian population from that territory. This is not true and this was confirmed by the Prosecution Witness ST-191 who attended the meeting himself. He testified that the only time when Mladic was in Teslic that was in late September or early October, and that was the only time that Mladic visited Teslic, that there were about 30 to 35 people attending that meeting. I would like to mention that at that time Mr. Radulovic had already left Teslic. When Witness 191 was faced with this document, the witness said that nothing had been said at the meeting about ethnic cleansing and that the report is completely fabricated and that its contents completely false. The witness said nothing that is mentioned here did not happen at the meeting. That is on transcript page 18548. Lisica was also asked about the document and about that meeting at transcript page 26902. He was also asked about Mladic's diary. According to Mladic's diary, that meeting happened on the 5th of December. In paragraphs 922, the Prosecution says that ST-174 constantly complained to Zupljanin about the Serbian police that committed crimes against the non-Serbian population. We -- I already discussed the credibility of this witness at the very outset of my presentation, so I don't want to repeat myself. We're claiming that Mr. Zupljanin undertook a number of measures against such unlawful actions. The Prosecution witness ST-225 confirmed that he was a witness in the police investigation into the explosions and planting explosive devices on the houses of non-Serbs. He also supported the position of the Defence that it was the army that should have investigated the aforementioned incidents. He also confirmed that soldiers, when they were coming back from the front line, usually shot in the air and caused trouble. On one occasion they even set fire near Podpecna [phoen] mosque. When it comes to paragraph 923 and the red van which is mentioned in there, the Defence would like to recall the testimony of Witness ST-223, who stated in his testimony that in any case the police did whatever they could and he admitted that he was not absolutely sure whether there -- anything was done against those persons, whether they were, indeed, members of the army or perhaps the police. When he was faced with the evidence, according to which Zupljanin had ordered the arrest of Goran Gataric or Gavrin, for whom ST-223 believed that he was one of those who rode in the red van, later on it was established that Gavrin was a soldier and a report by the military police confirmed that he was arrested in 1993 on account of the crimes that he had committed in 1992. In paragraph 799, it is stated that Zupljanin, when he wanted to do so, could undertake certain measures, and the example of Teslic is mentioned and the arrest of the Mice Group. I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to pay attention to the part of the testimony of Witness Radulovic on transcript pages 11087 and 11088 where he explained the difference where he said why it was possible in Teslic and not in Prijedor, primarily in Prijedor, and in other regions as well. In paragraph 803 there is a reference to the fact that Zupljanin had given authority to SJBs to investigate grave crimes. It was not Zupljanin's decision. It was the government of the Republika Srpska that made the decision. L55 says that basic courts became responsible for all crimes, and, in line with that, basic courts became competent for investigation of all the crimes, so the SJBs were supposed to investigate all crimes including the gravest of crimes. As for the operative plan, or paragraph 804, it is stated in here that Mr. Zupljanin, although he already had information from two previous reports about the number of crimes committed in the course of April, he did not approval the plan before the 25th of May. I invite the Trial Chamber to carefully inspect the document. I believe it is very important. It is stated in that document this was the plan to elucidate robberies, terrorism, extortions, and other such crimes, and that those crimes escalated in number in Banja Luka from the beginning of April of that year. In that paragraph, the Prosecution criticises Mr. Zupljanin for having done very little and that what he did was negligible. In that document, there's a detailed list of measures that were supposed to be taken. It is stated that over 40 people had to be arrested. It is stated how many crimes were committed. It is stated that 76 explosive devices were planted. Some very specific measures are listed as how things had to be done, and at the end of the document Mr. Zupljanin says that since the aforementioned persons organised themselves as members of the SOS, that they were well armed and some of them had even been mobilised into JNA units, their arrests had to be carried out by the units of the military police. In order to [indiscernible] the plan efficiently, things had to be co-ordinated with regular military courts. And, at the end, it is stated: "Until the moment the military prosecutor's office and the military courts are established, there are no conditions in place for the full-on implementation of the plan because these people are mostly military conscripts, former TO members, which is why civilian courts and prosecutor's office cannot be involved in the conduct of proceedings against them."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am going to say just a few words before the break. First, at page 13, line 18, of today's transcript, there's an imprecision. As it came in, it turns out as if Mr. Aleksic disagreed with what Ms. Butler said, and that was, of course, not the case. He agreed with what Ms. Butler said and disagreed with what the Prosecution had to say. Let me, Your Honours, turn to several matters arising from the 30 May closing arguments of the Prosecution, specifically page 27440, where the Prosecution say that in the case where a reserve policeman is taken off the list of the police and transferred to the army, that it may so happen that a member of the police who committed a disciplinary or criminal offence, upon transfer to the army, may commit a similar crime and since -- since the VRS was not privy to what sort of the conduct he had engaged in before joining the army. Now this statement is completely untrue. The evidence, documentary and the testimonies, confirm that whenever an individual was taken off the reserve police force and transferred to the army, this would be reflected in the personnel file which would also be sent to the army through the Ministry of Defence. Now, in view of the fact that the personnel file of every individual had to contain details about the individual's disciplinary and possible disciplinary procedures against him, this position expressed by the Prosecution does not reflect the actual state of affairs. Furthermore, at paragraph 738 of their final brief, the Prosecution cited Defence exhibit, 2D63. They discussed the fact where it was that the members of the special police unit ended up after the unit's disbandment. I established that in the English translation in e-court the first page of this document is missing. Can we call up 2D63 now, page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Krgovic speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at the first part where it says that most of the members of the former special detachment were within the war-time assignments of the VRS and not on the lists of the police force or any sort of special police that was allegedly set up by Zupljanin. And there is no evidence to prove that Zupljanin set up any special police units in the course of 1992, as of Autumn 1992, onto 1993. Your Honours, I would like to say a few words about Mr. Stojan Zupljanin's personality and character, and I will be sharing this topic with my learned friend, Ms. Butler. Perhaps we can take the break now so we can look into the part that we will share and see if we can reduce it somewhat and bring our closing arguments to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we would return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in their final trial brief and closing arguments, the Prosecution tried to represent Stojan Zupljanin as a person who was crucial and played a key role in the persecutions and murders. It is our position, Your Honours, that there is considerable or overwhelming evidence that refutes these positions advanced by the Prosecution, and I'm referring primarily to some of the key documents that my colleague Aleksic mentioned, including P2065, P355, P160, the last one being very important because it is the 11th of July speech by Mr. Zupljanin where he pin-pointed some of the key problems in the working of the MUP; among those things, for the first time a senior high-ranking officer pointed to the existence of camps, the prevailing poor conditions in them long before this became public knowledge. He indicated the problems that we addressed during this trial, the problems with the army, resubordination, the operation of the communications system, the fact that the judiciary was not working, and many other things. If Mr. Zupljanin voluntarily, as the Prosecution put it, participated in the development of a joint criminal plan, why did he address these issues on the 11th of July? Why did he advocate that better conditions be put in place? Why did he intercede and advocate that they be released? The crucial document that the Their Honours should bear in mind when deciding about the character of Mr. Zupljanin and his sentence is 2D25. Look at the start -- look at the beginning of the document, Your Honours, and find there how it is that Mr. Zupljanin described the situation in the area of responsibility of the Security Services Centre. He speaks about armed rebellion, acts of violence, crime, looting, flouting the law, civilian or civil disobedience and all the other occurrences that characterise the situation in Krajina at the time. What you will not find in any other document is to be found at page 2 of this document where he says that the situation, such as this one, creates fear among other ethnic groups and unavoidably causes ethnic division and a lack of confidence in the institutions of the system. Would this be the way that these matters would be addressed by a person who was an important member of the -- of a criminal enterprise? He does not hesitate to say at the bottom of the second page and at the top of the third page of this document and to criticise and draw the attention of the police in public security stations, to all these various facts. And, at the end, Your Honours, you will see that there are 11 items containing 11 orders that he issued in -- in the document. Namely, that the failure to obey any orders, including the army and Main Staff, would be contrary to the law; that no tasks should be taken on, such as to guard prisoners, who have been unlawfully detained; taking essential, resolute and uncompromising actions to shed light on or detect any crime present in stations; filing criminal reports to prosecutors; and, where there is no prosecutor's office active in one's area, reports should be filed to the second prosecutor closest to the area. A detailed analysis of this document will undoubtedly show that this is not the sort of the situation to which an old say would apply that the only necessary thing to fight evil would be for a good man not to do anything. Your Honours, in assessing the evidence, look at P601 and P595, P621, and P624. From these documents it will become clear to you that Mr. Zupljanin was committed to the maintenance of law and order for all individuals regardless of their religion or ethnicity, that he was not afraid to appoint to the unlawful activities on the part of his subordinates, or those who were supposed to be his subordinates, and that he did everything in his power to present such activities. Finally, I'd like to remind Their Honours of two events that shed light on the personality of Mr. Zupljanin. Namely, the events in Teslic, where Mr. Zupljanin secured the release from detention several hundred -- of several hundred Muslims and Croats in the course of the Mice action; and the incident along the Stanari-Teslic road where Mr. Zupljanin prevented the killing of 600 non-Serbs. The appropriate references are at pages of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Krgovic please repeat the reference slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2598 to 2599. Transcript pages 11020 and 11021. Your Honours, my brief presentation so far and the documents and exhibits I referred to did not reflect anything of the kind in this case or in the cases that are before the BH State Courts, what -- Zupljanin's words and Zupljanin's actions. That's what I meant. Your Honours, I have concluded my presentation. I will now give the floor to Ms. Butler who will be speaking about sentencing and some other legal issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. BUTLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I will now make some short submissions on matters of law and then sentencing, and that will conclude the presentation for the Zupljanin Defence team. In a criminal trial, Your Honours, there are many cumulative elements that must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Each and every one has to be proved, and if one fails, the whole case fails. We say that the Prosecution has not proved every single element of any of the modes of liability that they put in their indictment. Unfortunately, I don't have the luxury of time to go through the complex web of liability that is alleged against my client, but I will make some brief and I hope illustrative comments to demonstrate my point in relation to joint criminal enterprise in relation to command responsibility, and aiding and abetting. For the sake of clarity, the Defence also maintain that the Prosecution is a long way off proving the other modes of liability charged in the indictment; that is, planning, instigating, and ordering. The Prosecution themselves may also recognise this, as despite the more than 1.000 paragraphs in their beautifully put final brief and despite having a number of specific sections dealing with modes of liability, there is no discussion of Mr. Zupljanin's apparent liability pursuant to the doctrines of planning, instigating, or ordering. It is the Defence submission that this omission speaks volumes about the strength of the Prosecution's evidence on these modes. I will turn first to joint criminal enterprise, or JCE. For better or for worse, this doctrine is now part of the landscape of this Tribunal. However, as the Appeals Chamber has taken care to emphasise in the Brdjanin case, the doctrine may not be applied so as to give rise to guilt by mere social. That is not enough. As the Appeals Chamber was keen to highlight in that case: All elements of the case must be proved by the Prosecution beyond a reasonable doubt. In her submissions, my learned friend, Ms. Korner, acknowledged that there is no direct evidence of Zupljanin's alleged discriminatory attitude towards non-Serbs. As she put it at transcript T27365 Zupljanin was not a Brdjanin, he wasn't a Vukic, he wasn't a Kalinic. I can see my learned friend shaking her head and I will correct that. She did go on to assert that if you look at his actions, they have no other explanation but of his wholehearted endorsement of and involvement in a Bosnian Serb criminal plan. Now, Your Honours will be well aware of the test for conviction for a JCE where it relies upon circumstantial evidence. We say, and this has been affirmed recently by the Haradinaj Trial Judgement, that participation in a JCE, when relied upon by some circumstantial evidence, must be the only reasonable conclusion on the evidence. Your Honour, in our respective submission, the Prosecution has not proved to the requisite standard that there is no other theory that could explain Mr. Zupljanin's conduct except for his participation in a JCE. Despite all their hard work, despite all their diligence, the Prosecution evidence just does not withstand scrutiny on this issue. This is because the Defence suggest that Mr. Zupljanin's good character is such that it tends to negate the suggestion that he willingly participated in a JCE. Now, we accept wholeheartedly Mr. Hannis's observation yesterday that good character is not a Defence to the charges. That's not what we are saying. What we are saying is that if a person is of good character, and, specifically, with respect to Mr. Zupljanin, is known to be non-discriminatory, that is both relevant and probative for the purpose of determining his proclivity to participate in a common criminal plan. Your Honours will undoubtedly recall the host of evidence highlighted in paragraphs 56 to 75 of our final brief which originated from both Prosecution and Defence witnesses and which illustrates what we say is the true and non-discriminatory character of my client. We say that this is significant evidence and it cannot be readily dismissed. When Your Honours deliberate on the evidence in this case, we would ask you to ask yourself: Is Stojan Zupljanin the kind of man with a burning hatred of non-Serbs? Is he the kind of man who would killing commit the kinds of heinous acts that are alleged by the Prosecution to be part of this JCE? Is it really possible to reconcile the police officer, described by many as a person of the utmost integrity, who went out of his way to treat all religions and ethnicities equally and he took care during the war to ensure that businesses of local Muslims thrived, is it really possible to reconcile that officer of the law with the lackadaisical, uncaring and highly prejudiced individual described by the Prosecution? Your Honours, a JCE theory, however much work has done upon it, however much analysis, however many hours are spent on it, should not be accepted by strength of repetition. In our respectful submission, the evidence in this case does not show that there is no other explanation for Mr. Zupljanin's conduct but for his participation in a JCE. I will deal next with the issue of command responsibility. Your Honours will be well aware that the concept did not evolve as a matter of strict liability whereby a commander is responsible for every single act by every single person, whether the commander knows about that act or no. The Celebici Trial Chamber said on this subject at paragraph 377 of its Judgement: "Great care must be taken, lest an injustice be committed in holding individuals responsible for the acts of others in situation where the link of control is absent or too remote." To determine whether Mr. Zupljanin was able to exercise effective control in the chaotic situation that existed in the Krajina in 1992, the Trial Chamber should not rely solely on his legal authority but must instead study the evidence as to what practical control he had over his purported subordinates. We note that the Prosecution themselves accept at transcript page 27330 that the course of the relationships between the political, the army, and the police, did not always run smoothly. It is our case that in actual fact the relationship between these three bodies was so fractured and disproportionate in terms of the real power that the Crisis Staffs and the army had, that it completely subjugated Mr. Zupljanin' authority over local police, who, by law, were meant to be his subordinates. We say that the practice of resubordination of my police officers to the army to engage in combat tasks is problematic for the Prosecution's case on command responsibility. This is because any confusion as to the chain of command has the effect of negating the existence of effective control. We say that this raises a reasonable doubt as to whether Mr. Zupljanin had effective control over the perpetrators of the crimes. I will deal now with the matters raised on Wednesday in the course of Mr. Olmsted's well-put submissions. The particular references are at transcript page 27441 to 27443. In his submissions, Mr. Olmsted referred to what he regarded as persuasive authority from the Popovic Trial Judgement. In that authority, Mr. Borovcanin was found to have retained effective control over RS MUP police special units even when they were resubordinated and were committing crimes in Potocari. In the interests of time, I won't read out the full extracts from that Judgement, but I would certainly invite Your Honours to have a look at that in due course. When one does, one can see that Mr. Olmsted is quite correct to note that the Trial Chamber, in paragraph 1568 of that case, did recall the principle of unity of command under which MUP forces resubordinated to the VRS retained their internal chain of command. They did find that. However, that case can be readily distinguished on facts from that of Mr. Zupljanin. Quite apart from the evidence about Mr. Borovcanin's receipt of a contemporaneous report from the units in question and putting to one side his presence in Potocari at the relevant times, paragraphs 1567 and 1568 of the Borovcanin Judgement indicate that Mr. Borovcanin gave an interview to the Prosecutor in which he did not contest that the troops in question were under his command and control. Likewise, the evidence cited in those paragraphs indicates that Mr. Borovcanin's orders were, in fact, followed by those subordinate units. We suggest that these facts are very different to those in the present case where we say that: First, Mr. Zupljanin's command and control of his alleged subordinates is contested; and, second, in practice, Mr. Zupljanin's orders were not actually followed by those subordinates. The next issue addressed by Mr. Olmsted was in relation to Your Honour Judge Hall's question about the Tribunal's case law supporting the proposition that a subordinate can be under the command of more than one superior and that each said superior can be held responsible for the subordinate's crimes. Now, in answer to that question, Mr. Olmsted cited the case of Strugar for this proposition at paragraph 367. Now, it may be an error on the transcript, but from my study of the Judgement, I think he must have been referring to paragraph 365 because in that paragraph, the Trial Chamber recalled that: "The test of effective control ... implies that more than one person can be held responsible for the same crime committed by a subordinate." But, if one has a look at the context to that quote, so, specifically, if you read paragraphs 361 to 366 of that Judgement with care, it's plain that the Strugar Judgement, Strugar Trial Chamber, in fact, as it says in terms in paragraph 361, was concerned with the issue of whether a commander may be found responsible for the crimes committed by a subordinate two levels down in the chain of command. So they were talking about a vertical chain of command. It was specifically not concerned with the proposition which Mr. Olmsted seeks to establish; namely, that parallel chains of command are recognised in the case law of this Tribunal. Turning back to command responsibility more generally. In conclusion, quite apart from the issue of effective control, given the insufficient evidence to prove beyond a reasonable doubt Mr. Zupljanin's knowledge of crimes and his failure to take measure to prevent and punish those crimes, we say that he cannot, therefore, be found liable pursuant to this mode of liability. I will deal now with aiding and abetting. The Prosecution maintain that Mr. Zupljanin is also liable for aiding and abetting the crimes charged in the indictment by way of both his actions and omissions. I will deal with both allegations relatively shortly. First, in relation to his actions, it is plan that the elements for this mode of liability cannot be made out on the evidence. There is no evidence proving beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Zupljanin's acts had a substantial effect on the commission of the crimes. It is also not proved that Mr. Zupljanin took a decision to act in the way he did in 1992, in the knowledge that he would be supporting the individuals committing indictment offences. Indeed, the evidence, as was outlined in our final brief as well as during these closing submissions, shows the very opposite. Mr. Zupljanin was horrified by any crimes he heard about. He took steps to try and prevent these occurrences and to try and punish the perpetrators. Second, in relation to aiding and abetting by omission, the Trial Chamber will be very well aware of the limited jurisprudence to date on this mode of liability. It is the Defence submission that if one scrutinises the Borovcanin Trial Judgement, which is the leading Judgement on this area, particularly at paragraphs 1543 to 1563, that it is immediately obvious that the alleged omissions of Mr. Zupljanin in this case are of a wholly different scale to the alleged omissions -- well, to the admissions, I'm sorry, of Mr. Borovcanin in relation to the massacre at the Kravica warehouse. For these reasons, we say that the elements of aiding and abetting, either by action or omission, are not made out. My final submissions refer to -- relate to the issue of sentence. For the sake of clarity, it remains the position of the Defence of Stojan Zupljanin that our client is not guilt, and that the only proper verdict that you may return in relation to the charges is that of an acquittal. Although we still proclaim the innocence of our client, due to the Tribunal's settled - yet still very unfortunate - practice of conflating submissions as to conviction and sentence, we will take this opportunity now to make some brief remarks. We note in the Prosecution's final brief at paragraph 999 that it says "both men," presumably meaning Stanisic and Zupljanin, are responsible for crimes committed "in a series of at least 52 detention facilities." The Prosecution make no attempt to distinguish between the crimes for which Mr. Zupljanin is charged, which relate to 22 detention facilities, and the other crimes mentioned in the indictment for which he is not alleged to have been involved in any way, shape, or form. This tarring of Mr. Zupljanin with crimes for which he is not charged must be a mistake. It is certainly a regrettable one. It is trite law to state, of course, that the Trial Chamber must consider the exact role of each individual accused before determining an appropriate sentence. The Trial Chamber must carefully take into account both their intention as well as their acts and omissions. Bearing this in mind, even taking the Prosecution case at its highest, for the Prosecution to suggest that Stojan Zupljanin should receive a sentence of life imprisonment, we say is nothing short of absurd. Not one of the more than a dozen individuals convicted at this Tribunal for crimes taking place in the Krajina have had a life sentence upheld on appeal. Not one. This kind of blanket submission as to the maximum available penalty without any form of tailoring to the crimes charged, without any guidance by reference to comparative sentenced handed out at the Tribunal for similar crimes is of no help whatsoever to a Trial Chamber trying to come to a fair and just outcome. Sentences thus far handed out to individuals for crimes committed in the Krajina region following a contested trial range from 40 years at the highest end. That was for Stakic who was found to have orchestrated and actively participated in the tragic events taking place at Prijedor. And, at the low end, they go right down to five years and for that Prcac, a retired police officer working at Omarska whose silence in the face of crimes committed there was found to have given tacit support to the perpetrators. Your Honours, we say that even if, contrary to all our submissions, you find that Stojan Zupljanin has played a part in the allegations made against them, then in light of the lack of direct evidence as to his direct involvement in those crimes, in the light of his efforts to prevent and punish those crimes, and in light of his good character and his lack of discrimination against non-Serbs, we would say that a punishment at the very lowest end of that spectrum is the right disposition of this case. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Butler. I take it, Mr. Krgovic, that that was the final word from the Defence of Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes our closing arguments. I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that my client, Stojan Zupljanin, would like to address Their Honours to make a few points, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. We have been alerted to that. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we inquire of counsel for the Prosecution as to whether they have any submissions to make by way of rebuttal in accordance with Rule 86(A), the Chamber, in the person of Judge Harhoff, has one matter which he would seek counsel for the Prosecution to explicate.

utterances.text: Thank you. There is a discussion about this in several instances, and we would just wish to know what the Prosecution's position is on this matter, if possible. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]... we're slightly taken by surprise by that, and if Your Honours would just give us a moment or so to discuss that.

utterances.text: Should we rise?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes. [Microphone not activated] moment when you say, Could we perhaps ask for a little clarification, because Mr. Olmsted has, in fact -- is going to deal with the matters that were the cause of some discussion yesterday in relation to the resubordination and dual control - we hadn't anticipated this question - could, perhaps, we inquire which particular crimes Your Honour had in mind, as requiring dolus specialus.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Persecution, yes. Your Honours, could we come back to that? It strikes me we're going to go beyond, regrettably, the second break, in any event, with the matters that -- and we would welcome the chance to discuss it over the break and then come back and give Your Honour an answer. Your Honours, can we deal with it in this way. As Your Honours know, two matters arose during the course of our submissions yesterday -- the day before yesterday. The first, in relation, as he have just mentioned, Mr. Olmsted's reference to, as it were, the dual chains of command with which we would wish to address you on now and which has been raised again by Mr. Krgovic and the Defence team for Zupljanin and then Mr. Hannis on this question of the Stanisic interview. However, I don't know, did Your Honours rule on whether Mr. Zupljanin could have a final word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I neglected to -- when I indicated that we were alerted to the application would be made, I should have said that the Chamber would allow him to have a word and that would be the -- the last thing before we formally close.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And coming back to the discussions that we would have had earlier in the week about the time for any wrap-up legal arguments, I suppose, subject to being correct, that Rule 86(A) to which I alluded earlier, that what we are doing now is conflating the two things. So, in other words, any -- the -- the -- any rebuttal, rejoinder that we would now hear would embrace those issues which -- to which counsel on both sides would have alluded earlier in the week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was about to say that. We -- we -- we do not seek to deal in rebuttal with any of the factual matters, those that have come up, and those that we objected to we have raised effectively during the course of argument. We simply seek to deal with the matters of law. So if Your Honours are content, then Mr. Olmsted can deal with the issue of the dual chains of command, as it were, and then Mr. Hannis can deal with the interview, and then I just have a few small points that arise from the final briefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Firstly, yesterday, Mr. Zecevic quoted my response to Judge Hall's question to suggest that the Prosecution had changed its position with regard to resubordination, that we were now taking the position that resubordination applied whenever the police were participating in combat operations on the front lines. That is not the position of the Prosecution. It has never been the position of the Prosecution. We have continuously maintained throughout the trial that resubordination could only occur when the police were engaged in combat operation along the front lines; however, not all instances in which the police did engage in combat operations along the front lines were instances where they were resubordinated to the army. Rather, resubordination rarely occurred during the indictment period, and it did not occur in relation to any of the crimes charged in the indictment. And I just point out that the CSB Banja Luka's year-end report, P624, makes the distinction between police participation in combat independently, and police participation in combat as a resubordinated unit to the army. So just to make that clear. And we refer the Trial Chamber to paragraphs 871 to 880 of our final brief where we make clear our position and the evidence on this issue. The legal submission I was making on behalf of the Prosecution Wednesday was that even if the Chamber were to find that with regard to a crime charged in the indictment a particular police unit was resubordinated to the military, that does not mean, as a matter of law, that the accused were no longer the superiors of that police unit for purposes of command responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute. Rather, under command responsibility, a perpetrator can have more than one superior who has effective control over that perpetrator, and each of those superiors can be held criminally liable for that perpetrator's crimes. There are, essentially, what I would break down into two categories of Tribunal cases that support this argument. First, there are a number of cases against military accused which established that perpetrators can have more than one superior both within the same military chain of command as well as in multiple chains of command, and I refer the Trial Chamber in this case to Strugar Trial Judgement, paragraph 365; the Naletilic Trial Judgement, paragraph 69; and the Blaskic Trial Judgement at paragraph 303. Second, there is a line of cases against civilian accused which established that a -- that perpetrators can have more than one superior within separate chains of command of different organs. In particular, the perpetrators can have a civilian superior as well as an army superior, and I refer you to the Aleksovski paragraph 106; the Colonel Jelac Trial Judgement, paragraphs 93 to 107; as well as the Popovic Trial Judgement, the paragraphs I provided on Wednesday. Let's take the Aleksovski case. The accused in that case was the civilian warden of a prison in Lasva valley. As a Defence, he argued that the guards at the prison who committed the war crimes at issue were members of military police and therefore he had no superior responsibility over them. The guards had their own military chain of command that was responsibility for their actions. The Trial Chamber disagreed finding at paragraph 106: "The issue whether the guards came concurrently under another authority, such as the military police commander, in no way detracts from the fact that the accused was their superior within the confines of the Kaonik prison." Now, the Prosecution submits that an analogy can be drawn between that case at what occurred in Manjaca camp in 1992. Even if the Trial Chamber were to accept the Defence argument that the police officers from Sanski Most and Kljuc who were sent to Manjaca by CSB Banja Luka to assist with guarding that facility, were resubordinated on each occasion, each shift that they went to that facility, it does not automatically follow that their only superior was Colonel Popovic, the camp commander. While at the camp, the colonel undoubtedly gave the police officers who were performing guard duties orders and instructions. However, the police superiors also maintained effective control over these police guards, determining which police officers to send to Manjaca and for how long, and as the Prosecution submits, they exercise ultimate disciplinary and criminal jurisdiction over these police officers. Now, in the Popovic case, the accused Borovcanin was the RS MUP deputy commander of a joint MUP force that included several police companies that participated with the VRS in operations in Srebrenica in July 1995. As a Defence, he argued that one of the police companies, the Jahorina recruits, was under the command of the VRS Bratunac Brigade security organ, while committing crimes in Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July. The Trial Chamber in this case found that even though the Jahorina recruits were resubordinated to the army, Borovcanin maintained effective control over these police officers. In making this finding, the Trial Chamber relied on -- in part, Article 14 of the 1994 RS Law on the Implementation of the Law on Internal Affairs During an Imminent Threat of War or State of War. That is it L317 in our case. And that law states, Article 14: "Police units shall be under the direct command of a commander who is a member of the Ministry of Interior. During the time they are resubordinated to the Army of Republika Srpska, they shall retain their organisation and may not be split up or separated." The Trial Chamber then found, as Ms. Butler pointed out, that this law established a unity of command principle of MUP forces resubordinated to the VRS. And that's at paragraph 1567. The Prosecution submits that this 1994 law which I just quoted is nearly identical to Stanisic's 15 May 1992 order establishing the police war units which required that if those units were subordinated and they weren't always subordinated, but if they were, the ministry units shall be under the direct command of certain ministry officials. Now, to cite that is 1D46. Now, as Ms. Butler attempted to do, of course, if you look at these cases that I've just mentioned, you will find factual distinctions. That is inevitable. This case that we have before us is unique in that we are charging high-level police officials for the conduct for perpetrators at quite a low level. But what we do submit is that this jurisprudence establishes the general legal principles that Your Honours should use as a guide when you are coming -- when you are addressing these, to a certain degree, novel legal issues with regard to resubordination. And we submit that the underlying point of this jurisprudence is that the concept of resubordination or unity of command are not decisive of the accused's command responsibility. What is decisive is whether the accused could exercise effective control over their subordinates. This is a question of fact, and, as the Prosecution has explained throughout its final brief and in its closing arguments, this has been established by the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honours, Before you hear from Mr. Hannis, do you want to hear from the other side on any of these matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think it would be more efficient to hear all of the Prosecution's submissions and then we hear from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, good morning. I just want to talk briefly about the issues raised concerning comments about Mr. Stanisic' suspect interview with the OTP in 2007. This is -- this is not in the nature of a comment of the kind prohibited by the Statute as held in Celebici. What this was about was what Mico Stanisic said and what he left unsaid during his 2007 suspect interview. And you'll recall that was an interview that was done with his counsel present. You can read in the interview that he was advised of all his rights and reminded of those rights each and every day of the interview. He freely waived those rights and agreed that his statement could be used at trial. He answered some questions but didn't answer all questions. He said there were some matters he didn't want to talk about. Mr. Zecevic has tried to claim that since we, the Prosecution, put the interview into evidence via a bar table motion, that means we vouch for the truth of its contents. That's not exactly correct, Your Honour. We don't. And I dare say we never said that. You can see in our bar table motion 2nd December 2010, his interview was 65 ter number 2827.01 through 2827.14. It's listed in Annex A to the motion which is at, I think it's the Registry's page number D, as in David, 10335. And the column in the table that is entitled: Relevance to case issues, we said that his interview was "the interview conducted under caution with the accused, Mico Stanisic, provides evidence of his position on many issues of relevance to this trial." That's all it said. Had we -- and, frankly, Your Honour, had we believed that everything he said in his interview was true, we would have been ethically bound to dismiss the indictment because he has claimed he was innocent. This is being offered to prove many other matters. And also the issue about whether we decided to tender it into evidence you should be aware that there's ICTR jurisprudence in a case whose name I will butcher, it is Ndayambaje, N-d-a-y-a-m-b-a-j-e, et al. My apologies for my pronunciation. It is ICTR 98-42-T. The 15th of May, 2006. It appears to hold that if the Prosecution does not tender such a statement in its case, it may be precluded from using the contents or the substance of such a statement in the Defence case, and in the event that the accused did not testify in a situation like that, the Prosecution wouldn't be able to use it at all. Now by not objecting to use of his statement at trial, Mico Stanisic put his credibility at issue. And it's not unfair or inappropriate for you to consider what he said and what he left unsaid or refused to say at the time of that interview when you decide what weight to give his interview in whole or regarding specific parts of that interview. I would just indicate I come from a jurisdiction where the general rule is that hearsay is not admissible, as opposed to here, hearsay is generally admissible. In -- in the system in the US, an out-of-court statement of a witness is hearsay and generally not admissible, but there's an exception for admissions by a party opponent in a civil case or a criminal case. They are defined as being not hearsay, and the theory is that if a party admits something that's contrary to his interest, his pecuniary interest or his penal interest, it is more reliable than self-serving statements. We believe that in this situation it is entirely appropriate for you to consider claims made by Mico Stanisic in his interview which neither panned out in determine what weight to give his words. Contrary to what Mr. Zecevic has tried to assert, that is, that everything he said in 2007 was true and turned out to match precisely the evidence presented at trial, that's simply not so. We gave you one example earlier in closing, his claim that between April and September 1992, before the autonomous regions were -- were banned in September, he said: "No CSB or SJB chief ever cited or relied on one of his or his assistant minister's orders." That is absolutely not true. We showed you three specific examples and there are many more. Finally, he didn't have to speak at all. He had an absolute right not to speak to the Prosecution but when he voluntarily and knowingly waived that right and proceeded to selectively answer some questions but not others, he cannot preclude the Prosecution from arguing or you Judges from considering that selectivity in 2007 in deciding what weight to give that total evidence. That's our submission. Thank you for hearing me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- can I say straight away, of course, our -- our first submission on that is that all the crimes are within the -- the original JCE, but in the alternative that the -- the -- the crimes outside those of forcible transfer and deportation come within JCE 3. The Trial Chamber in Brdjanin at the Rule 98 stage had, in fact, dismissed the charges of genocide, and that was -- there was an appeal on the basis that that was a erroneous decision in law. And the Appeals Chamber on the 19th of March, 2004, held as follows: They, first of all, dealt with an accused who enters into a joint criminal enterprise to commit the crime of forcible transfer, obviously shares the intent of the direct perpetrators to commit that crime. However, if the Prosecution can establish that the direct perpetrator, in fact, committed a different crime and that the accused was aware that the different crime was a natural and foreseeable consequence of the agreement to forcibly transfer, then the accused can be convicted of that different offence. And they go on to deal with genocide. And then paragraph 7, as a mode of liability, the third category of joint criminal enterprise is no different from other forms of criminal liability which do not require proof of intent to commit a crime on the part of the accused before criminal liability attaches. Your Honour, that was most recently cited in the Karadzic case of one of the early legal decisions. So, Your Honour, that's the situation, we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And does that in the Prosecution's opinion cover cases where the additional -- the additional foreseeable crime, was a crime that carries a special intent?

utterances.text: Yes. This actually dealt with genocide and you can't have more of a special intent than genocide.
