utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for that. And while we're on that, can I -- it is rather more factual but dealing with Ms. Butler's review of the sentences. The -- the sentence that was passed on Mr. Brdjanin, it was originally was 35 years - she didn't mention that - but reduced to 32 on appeal. Your Honours, may I then turn, as I say, very quickly to some of the more minor legal issue that have arisen from the final briefs of the accused. Your Honours, starting with Stanisic, please. At paragraph 7 of their final brief -- sorry. Yes, paragraph 7. The final sentence there states, they're dealing with, in particular, intercept evidence, and the CHS, and end off by saying that: "Evidence not proved to be authentic beyond a reasonable doubt would be granted no weight at the end of a trial." And they cite for this proposition, Brdjanin and Popovic. Your Honours, in fact, proof beyond a reasonable doubt applies to facts not evidence, and only though facts upon which a conviction or sentence depends. And the case on that is the Appeals Judgement, Milosevic, paragraph 20. Obviously interlocutory appeal. Proof beyond a reasonable doubt applies to facts, as I said, and, for example, an element of the crime or a mode of responsibility or a fact indispensable to entering a conviction and, Your Honours, the cite for that is Halilovic Appeals Judgement, paragraph 125. Your Honours, in paragraph 10, and I think this was just an error possibly. They deal with the actual burden and standard of proof. They rightly deal with the fact that it has to be a reasonable doubt until the penultimate sentence at paragraph 10 where they say: "If at the conclusion of proceed there is any doubt that the Prosecution has established the case against the accused, the accused is entitled to the benefit of that doubt." It is, of course, any reasonable doubt not fanciful or the like. As I say, I think that was just a drafting error. Your Honours, still on the Stanisic brief, if one looks at paragraph -- just to get them in order -- slightly. Yes, paragraph 211 of the Stanisic brief. There, they deal -- this is the part of the brief that deals with resubordination and its consequences. And at the end of that paragraph, on page 84, they say: "International law governing armed conflicts recognising that members of the police may be incorporated into the armed force through subordination to the army and that subordinate members of the police lose their status as civilian policemen and gain the status of military personnel and thereby become legitimate targets." And they quote one of their documents plus Lisica. But, in fact, Your Honours, international law does not support this argument that the accused lost effective control of the MUP units once incorporated into the armed forces. The relevant provision which is not cited here is Additional Protocol I, Article 43(3) and that merely notes that: "If police units are incorporated into a party's armed forces, notice must be given to the other parties to the international armed conflict. This procedure ensures that other parties know which police units can be treated as legitimate military targets." And there's the various commentaries on this. The -- adding to this, what they say is subordinate and subordination, it doesn't come into Article 43 at all. Because, obviously, this is a -- the question of which superior has the power, as Mr. Olmsted has dealt with, and duty to act is based not on international but on domestic law. And Your Honours, I think, finally, on the Stanisic brief, if one looks at paragraph 674. This is already one [indiscernible] one topic. They state the -- the existence of de jure authority is not synonymous with effective control. It does not necessarily imply de facto authority, nor does it create a presumption of effective control. And they cite Halilovic and Oric. Instead the inquiry should focus on the de facto relationship between the alleged superior and subordinate. However, Your Honours, what they don't cite and this also arises from the Oric case, and also, like Mr. Hannis, I have even more difficulty with Rwandan names than I do with Bosnian. It's a case called N-t-a-b-a-k-u-z-e Appeals Judgement at paragraph 169. It can be -- de -- de jure authority can be an indicator of effective control. At paragraph 681, they distinguish between a non-military superior and a military superior and they quote the Rome Statute. Your Honours, in our submission, there are is no separate mens rea for civilian superiors. The same mens rea requirement applies to both civilian and military superiors. The cases on that point are Djordjevic, Milutinovic, another Rwandan case - both of them Trial Judgements, I should add, obviously - this one is an Appeals Judgement B-a-g-i-l-i-s-h-e-m-a, Appeals Judgement, paragraph 35. And we submit that, although the Rome Statute gives different mens rea, that is not reflective of customary international law. Your Honours, those are the matters that we would deal with in the Stanisic brief. In respect of the Zupljanin brief. Your Honours, the first is paragraph 24. At the end, they're dealing with planning as a mode of liability. At the end of that paragraph, they say: "The defendant must be proven to have possessed the state of mind required by the underlying offence with which he is charged and to have directly or indirectly intended that the crime in question be committed." Your Honours, we say that the mens rea for planning is -- is a direct intent to plan a crime, or an awareness of the substantial likelihood that a crime will be committed in the execution of the acts or omissions planned. Again, it's the Milosevic Appeal Judgement, paragraph 268; and Kordic Appeals Judgement, paragraphs 29 and 31, which are not cited in the cites to that sentence in the brief. Next, Your Honours, the question of evidence outside the indictment period, at paragraphs 55 and 60, I think it is. Yes. Your Honours, they assert that it is impermissible - in paragraph 55 - for the Trial Chamber to give consideration to any events subsequent to the indictment period in determining his responsibility for acts taking place between the 1st of April and the 31st of December. Your Honours, we say that is -- that is really incorrect. Your Honours, Your Honours are entitled to look at evidence outside the indictment period. He cannot be held liable for any actions that he took in 1991 or 1993, but we say - and we say that's what the law says - that it can be evidence in support of other evidence which shows his actions in 1992 were criminal, and it goes further than just the mens rea itself. And, Your Honours, we set it out in paragraphs 714 to 717 of our brief because we say his actions in 1991, for example, are directly referable to his participation in the common plan. Just let me check. I think there was one more paragraph in respect of ... Oh, yes, sorry, Your Honours. I should -- I -- if we go back to paragraph 21. It started with that. In fact, this is very much along the lines of a question Judge Harhoff asked us. The Defence submit that in respect of JCE 3, he wasn't aware, et cetera, but that these were a natural and foreseeable consequence of the alleged JCE. Such crimes, it is said, are of a wholly different nature to acts of forcible transfer or deportation. They were either completely outside the JCE with which is he charged or formed part of an expanded JCE to commit acts of revenge. Your Honours, obviously what amounts to the JCE 3 crimes in a particular case is a factual question, but the crimes that we have charged of persecution, extermination, murder, torture, cruel treatment have already been found to be the natural and foreseeable consequences in many cases in -- before these Tribunals of one where the actual intention was that to forcibly transfer or deport. And we take leave to differ with the assertion that these crimes are of a wholly different nature to such an accident that they cannot be JCE crimes. And Your Honours, there's a host of different cases that support that. So, Your Honours, those are the matters that we would wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, I will speak in Serbian. [Interpretation] Your Honours, the position of the Defence with regard to the claims and positions presented by Mr. Olmsted is this: We absolutely do not agree with these claims and positions, and I will explain why. Mr. Olmsted rightly observes that there were two issues at stake here. The first issue is this: Can several superior persons have the same command responsibility for the acts committed by one subordinate? We agree that they can. However, Your Honours, we are talking about a company commander, a battalion commander, a brigade commander. The three of them are parts of the same chain, and all three of them can be held responsible for the actions or acts committed by a soldier in that company. And that is the situation, Your Honours, which applies to Strugar, as well as to Naletilic, as well as to Blaskic and Popovic. Why does it apply to Popovic? The answer is simple, Your Honours. When you read the Trial Judgement in the Popovic case, it says there that Borovcanin received an order from the minister to take the special unit and to report to Krstic to be resubordinated to General Krstic when he gets there. At that moment when he, as the commander of the police unit, is resubordinated to General Krstic, he gets a military superior who is above him. At that moment, he enters a military structure, and the distinction between him and any other company commander or battalion commander in the Army of Republika Srpska at that moment ceases to exist. It simply does not exist anymore. He becomes an element of the command structure of the army. Claims proffered by Mr. Olmsted apply to an entirely different situation. I don't have the exact reference number. However, he spoke on page 48 of today's transcript about Borovcanin, and he says that Borovcanin was found to be responsible for -- please bear with me. For a unit from Mount Jahorina which was under the command of the Bratunac Brigade on the 12th and the 13th of July. Your Honours, this is an identical situation. Those soldiers, those troops, or, rather, those policemen who are resubordinated to the military, we claim, and the law provides for them to become military conscripts of -- or soldiers. They were members of his unit, under his command, and he resubordinated that entire unit, together with himself, to the army. At one point in time, one part of that whole unit, several soldiers from that unit, went and joined another unit of the Army of Republika Srpska and committed a crime, and the Trial Chamber found him guilty. However, in that case, he was part of the military hierarchy, and he had nothing whatsoever to do with the Ministry of Defence at that moment when the crime was committed. And that is the gist of the whole matter. The fact that Borovcanin, before that and after that, was a member of the Ministry of Defence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction: The Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- at the moment when the crimes were committed, the same crimes for which he was found guilty, he was a member of the Army of Republika Srpska because he was resubordinated [as interpreted] to them, and he was part of that command chain, and that's why he was found guilty and convicted. The second issue, Your Honours, is the issue addressed by Mr. Olmsted on pages 47 and 48 of today's transcript. He spoke about two parallel, different chains of command, whereby there is a civilian authority or superior, as well as a military authority or a military superior. What Mr. Olmsted omits to observe in the Judgements or perhaps omits to mention here is a very clear position proffered by the Trial Chambers in those cases, and I will quote that position: "A perpetrator must obviously and clearly," and I underline obviously and clearly, "be within the hierarchical chain of command of the accused." And this is the situation that we're talking about. They found that the prison warden was obviously and clearly superior to those who committed the crime at the moment when the crime was committed. And this is a fact that was established. And we cannot draw any parallels with this case. We are not talking about dual authority or double authority. In that sense, the Prosecutor's assertion that what is at issue here are general legal principles that you should be govern -- governed by and that you should influence your decision-making process when you are considering these facts is incorrect. In general terms, and when we're talking about a general legal principle, we have to admit that, according to the doctrine of command responsibility, there is no possibility to have two different commanders belonging to two different chains of command. It can happen only - and I repeat, only - if all the commanders belong to one vertical line and chain of command. At the end of the day, the gist of the matter, when it comes to effective control, that, in theory, Your Honours -- it is theoretically impossible to have two different chains of effective control, two lines of effective controls, because one line and somebody in that line can say, You go to the left; whereas, the other person in the other line of command can say, You go to the right. Who is that person or that line that holds effective control? There's no possibility for two commanders to have effective control because it may happen that the two of them issued two contradictory orders at the same time. According to the theory of command responsibility, there should be just one, only one person, who was effective control. And what the jurisprudence of this Tribunal says and what the theory says is that, at the moment when a crime is committed, that person who has effective control, at that moment, is the person who should be held responsible and accountable for that crime.

Another way in which these types of acts can be taken into account is for the mens rea of the particular accused person. And another way is for clarifying the context to the crimes.
